text: Hi, everyone. I'm Brooke Longfox.
I'm a data curation scientist at MorphoBank, and this work
on, Is Artificial Intelligence Amplifying
Paleontology's Reproducibility Problem?
has been done with Mark Young, who's the editor-in-chief at Historical
Biology.
I wanted to start off by saying that this is not an argument against
AI in paleontology. I use AI-assisted approaches in
my own data curation work, and I think that they offer enormous
opportunities for making biodiversity data more accessible and
reusable.
However, AI is entering a field, paleontology,
that already has a significant reproducibility challenge.
So my argument and discussion here today is that AI can
amplify those challenges because it can transform
incomplete or maybe ambiguous information into structured
outputs that look ready for reuse.
So the question I want to ask is: what does our data
need to contain before we consider it truly AI-ready?
So paleontology is increasingly a digital and
data-intensive science.
A physical specimen can now be connected to images, occurrence,
and stratigraphic information, publications,
measurements, morphological matrices, and
analytical outputs. This is part of the broader idea of
the digital extended specimen. So the specimen becomes an anchor
within a network of linked digital information.
For example, I show here
an image of a skull from MorphoBank.
And what we have here is information
about where this skull is stored,
information about the photo itself, and then information about the
character. So this is the character state
information listed here.
This is giving an example of the connectivity,
and that's what we want. It makes information discoverable
and allows data generated for one study to support completely new
research.
But greater connectivity also means that problems in one
digital object can propagate much further downstream.
Before I discuss AI, I first want
to go over what is already happening with the data
being reused.
I see this quite directly through my work as a data editor for
Historical Biology.
As we've implemented a stronger journal data policy, the
same types of problems come up repeatedly.
I'm grouping them here into three broad categories.
This is availability. So can we get the data?
Then documentation. So if we get the file, can we
understand and reuse it? And finally, traceability.
Can we reconstruct where those data come from and how they produce the
published result?
So these are not AI problems, these are existing reproducibility
problems.
But AI matters because it changes what happens to those problems
next.
The first problem is simply availability.
Sometimes underlying data are never deposited.
Sometimes the manuscript says that no data exist, even though the
study is clearly reusing measurements,
images. It talks about models. It could talk about
specimens.
It could talk about photos that they took.
So we routinely encounter files on
personal websites. This could be cloud storage links rather
than persistent repositories, and repository records that are
private, incomplete, or inaccessible to reviewers.
So the first reproducibility barrier
is pretty basic, and it's, is there actually
data available after publication?
But availability alone is not enough.
We can have the file and still not have enough information to reuse it.
A dataset may have no README or data dictionary.
Abbreviations or exclusions may not be explained.
We may have a 3D model without enough information
about how it relates to the original specimen or imagery.
In a morphological matrix, character or state
definitions may be incomplete.
So a persistent identifier can tell me where the file
is, but it does not necessarily tell us what the
file means.
Then the third problem is traceability, and this is the one that
becomes particularly important for AI.
And this is, can we follow the chain from evidence to
result?
So sometimes a data availability statement does not correspond to the
files actually deposited.
A measurement or character score may not link clearly to its source.
A matrix may have been modified through multiple studies
without clearly documenting where individual characters or scores
originated.
And the version in the repository may not clearly be identifiable
as the version that produced the published analysis.
These individual pieces may all exist, but the linkage between them
has been lost. And now, if we introduce AI
into that environment,
basically we get uncertainty.
And AI can make that uncertainty look structured.
So this is the specific failure mode
I'm concerned about. One of AI's greatest strengths is that it can
take messy information and turn it into structure.
We can take an old PDF, a scanned table
with inconsistent terminology, a matrix,
and extract it, or normalize that information into a clean
dataset. But imagine that something in the source is
ambiguous.
Perhaps OCR shifted a column. Perhaps an
anatomical term was translated inconsistently.
Perhaps the original paper never documented why a
particular state was scored.
AI can still produce a perfectly formatted table.
That table may contain all the expected fields.
It might even pass schema validation.
It might be deposited in a repository, receive a DOI,
and then become ingested into another AI
program for more analysis.
So the structure has been improved, but the underlying scientific
uncertainty has not necessarily improved with it.
So that is the distinction I want to make between technical validity
and scientific validity.
A machine can tell us that a value has the correct format,
but that does not necessarily establish that the value accurately
represents the underlying biological evidence.
For example, morphological phylogenetics
gives an especially clear example.
So if we look at a character matrix that looks machine
friendly, we have taxa, characters, discrete values, zeros,
ones, twos, question marks.
If we take this example, for character 37, zero
is absent, one is present.
The values look objectively binary,
but producing it may have required considerable scientific reasoning.
What anatomical structures are we actually comparing?
Are those structures homologous?
Is something truly absent and not merely preserved?
Are we looking at different ontogenic stages?
Is the taxon polymorphic?
Are there any characters missing?
Is it biologically inapplicable?
So the cell in the matrix is structured, but the structure does
not contain all the reasoning that generated the cell.
AI may be able to extract an existing score or potentially infer
one, but responsible reuse will also need to
be able to be evaluated through evidence and
interpretation behind that score.
So in other words, character states can encode expert judgment,
not simply observations waiting to be extracted.
So this brings me to AI-ready data.
We already have several important pieces to the answer.
AI-ready data should be machine readable so computational systems can
actually work with them.
They should be FAIR, findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable.
They need sufficient documentation so methods and context are
explicit.
And they need validation, some defined process for checking that
output against technical and, where appropriately,
scientific criteria
But for interpretive data, I think we need to make one additional idea
explicit, and that's verifying it.
So can I take an individual assertion and trace it back to the
evidence that supports it?
Can I determine whether it was transcribed,
transformed, or inferred?
And can I tell whether a human expert or an automated process or
both validated it?
This is a different question from simply asking whether the file is structured.
And I think this gives us a practical path forward
toward robot-ready biodiversity data.
So first, I think we should define a use case.
So what exactly is the system doing?
Extracting information, transforming it, or making new inference?
Second, identify the information we need to preserve.
So the source method, the responsible agent, validation
status, and uncertainty.
Third is crosswalk existing standards.
This could be Darwin Core or other standards.
And then we need to identify the gaps.
So for example, can we currently record not just
that an assertion exists, but that it was
generated through an AI-assisted inference and then
confirmed by a domain expert?
So the goal is not to prevent machines from reusing our data.
It's to give the machines and the people enough context to reuse them
responsibly.
I'll end by thanking the TADWIG and symposium organizers
as well as researchers, editors, curators, and repository staff
whose day-to-day challenges helped shape this talk.
